records.name_note: NC State's page-title parenthetical and its stacked Common Name(s) field list the same four entries in alphabetical order — Coral Honeysuckle, Honeysuckle, Trumpet Honeysuckle, Woodbine — so its first entry is Coral Honeysuckle; its Description, Flower and Leaf prose nonetheless calls the species 'Trumpet honeysuckle'. MoBot's displayed Common Name field carries the single value 'trumpet honeysuckle' (a longer list sits behind a popup whose text exists only in the link's markup, so it is not quoted here). RHS's page title and plant-profile subtitle likewise lead with 'trumpet honeysuckle', with 'coral honeysuckle' appearing only in its separate Other common names field. Two of the three dedicated species pages therefore lead with Trumpet Honeysuckle and the third uses it throughout its body prose. Coral Honeysuckle is the first entry of NC State's alphabetized list and RHS's only other common name; Woodbine appears only in NC State's list.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS's Potentially harmful field states, verbatim: 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.  Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers' (double spaces and the absent final period are as rendered). This Pets language is unscoped — it does not name cats or dogs — so per the cat/dog scoping rule it does not by itself establish toxic_to_pets. NC State carries no Poisonous Plant Type tag and no Poison block for this species; its Fruit Description calls the berries only inedible ('The inedible rounded red berries form in late summer to early fall and can be ornamentally attractive.'), not poisonous, and does not mention pets or humans. The two sources agree the fruit should not be eaten but disagree on the rest of the plant: NC State's Uses (Ethnobotany) field records that 'It has been used medicinally (dried and smoked) for asthma. The juice of the plant (leaves ground by chewing) is beneficial in the treatment of bee stings. The leaves have been used as a decoction for coughs and sore throats,' which sits against RHS's blanket glove-and-protective-equipment handling warning. Separately, NC State flags a non-toxicity hazard on the same page: 'Fire Risk: This plant has a high flammability rating and should not be planted within the defensible space of your home,' with a structured Fire Risk Rating of 'high flammability.'
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the only toxicity evidence found (RHS's Potentially harmful field) uses generic, unscoped 'Pets' language that does not name cats or dogs specifically, and NC State carries no Poison block or Poisonous Plant Type tag for this species, so there is no admissible cat/dog-specific toxicity evidence either way.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists an open-ended Acid (<6.0) band and a closed-top Neutral (6.0-8.0) band, but RHS's pH field ('Acid or Alkaline or Neutral') accepts both acid and alkaline soils, so per the both-directions check neither a floor nor a ceiling is set.

water_regime left null: the only structured watering signal found (MoBot's 'Water: Medium') is mid-scale and, per rule, cannot itself support keep_moist; no admissible source frames watering for this species as a dry-down cadence, so water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are all left null (the day-interval fields also because this is an in-ground vine, not a potted plant framed on a day-interval schedule).

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's only numeric sun-hours figures ('6 or more hours', '2-6 hours') come from its site-wide light-category legend, not species-specific prose, and no other admissible source gives a species-specific hour figure.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, and chill_damage_f left null: no admissible source gives species-specific foot-candle, humidity percentage, target temperature, or cold-damage-onset figures for this species; NC State's USDA zone range (4a-9b) is a hardiness/survival rating, not an onset temperature.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength left null: NC State's Description only warns that 'High nitrogen fertilizer will produce foliage at the expense of flowers,' a fertilizer-type caution rather than a schedule, interval, or dilution strength.

records.name_note: NC State's page title and its Common Name(s) list carry three stacked entries in the same, alphabetical order (American Wisteria, Kentucky Wisteria, Texas Wisteria), so its first entry, American Wisteria, reflects alphabetical order. Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated single-species Plant Finder page displays one Common Name field, 'American wisteria,' with no Common Names tooltip/list control present on this page. Because MoBot's is a dedicated single-species page and its lead value matches the first (alphabetically ordered) entry in NC State's list, 'American Wisteria' is used as the common name here. RHS's dedicated species page (reached by the audit; the researcher's search had not surfaced it) is titled 'Wisteria frutescens | American wisteria', agreeing with the North American lead.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Poison block for Wisteria frutescens is filed under the heading 'Poisonous to Humans:' (i.e., the severity rating below is human-scoped, distinct from the separate Problems tags for cats/dogs/horses). Poison Severity: Medium. Poison Symptoms: 'Nausea, frequent vomiting, abdominal pain depression, and diarrhea can result from eating 1 or 2 seed pods.' Poison Toxic Principle: 'Saponin called wisterin, Lectin.' Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Seeds. NC State's Edibility field, however, reads: 'Ingestion of any part of the plant can cause discomfort. Its roots, bark, branches, fruits, and seeds contain triterpene-based saponins that can cause gastro-intestinal distress. The seeds also contain a molecule called canavanine.  When ingested, it can disrupt the synthesis of proteins, which in turn can result in an impairment of multiple life processes.' Separately, NC State's Problems field tags this species Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, and Problem for Horses (the horse tag names an animal outside the cat/dog scope but is co-listed with the cat and dog tags). RHS's Potentially harmful field for this species reads: 'Harmful if eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.  Pets: Harmful if eaten - for further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants' -- a handling warning NC State does not carry.
unknowns: RHS's dedicated species page (rhs.org.uk/plants/94290/wisteria-frutescens/details, title 'Wisteria frutescens | American wisteria', distinct from the 'Amethyst Falls' and 'Longwood Purple' cultivar pages) was reached by the audit after the researcher's search had not surfaced it; its title, Position and Potentially harmful fields are cited at landing. Its Name Status value was not captured, so scientific_name_accepted stays null.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null: NC State's Soil pH field for this species reads only the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band, which sets no floor or ceiling, and RHS's pH field (which the rules require checking in both directions before setting a Neutral-band ceiling/floor) could not be located for this species.

water_regime is left null: no admissible source gives a watering statement for this species. MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium,' which per the schema rules is mid-scale and cannot support keep_moist; it is noted here only as a disclosed data point, not as the basis for any regime value.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null: both NC State and MoBot say only that 'An application of fertilizer in early spring can also help stimulate flowering,' a word-based seasonal cadence with no literal day interval, month number, or dilution/strength fraction stated.

chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, day/night temperature fields, humidity fields, and light_fc/direct_sun_hours_max are left null: no admissible source for this species states numeric temperature thresholds, humidity requirements, foot-candle light levels, or a species-specific direct-sun-hours figure (NC State's Light field only carries the generic full-sun/partial-shade category legend, which the rules exclude as a source for direct_sun_hours_max).

Clemson HGIC (hgic.clemson.edu) and UF/IFAS (edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu) were searched for a Wisteria frutescens-specific factsheet but no accessible species page was found (search results and direct guessed URLs returned 404 or no matching content); Penn State, U Maryland, and UGA sources were not found to carry a dedicated American Wisteria page either. Only plants.ces.ncsu.edu and plantfinder.mobot.org supplied verified, species-confirmed content for this record.

records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) field lists six names alphabetically — American Bittersweet, Bittersweet, Climbing Bittersweet, False Bittersweet, Shrubby Bittersweet, Waxwork — and its first entry matches the first name in the page title parenthetical. American Bittersweet is used as the lead because two other dedicated single-species pages lead with it outright: RHS titles its page 'Celastrus scandens | American bittersweet' and lists the remaining names under 'Other common names,' and Missouri Botanical Garden's Common Name field reads 'American bittersweet' and states that 'American bittersweet is the generally accepted common name that is used today, in large part to distinguish this American native from its aggressive Asiatic relative, C. orbiculatus (Oriental bittersweet).' NC State's own description prose also opens with 'American bittersweet.' The 'bittersweet' name traces to Eurasian bittersweet nightshade (Solanum dulcamara): per MoBot, colonists applied it because the fruits resembled that nightshade's, and 'false bittersweet' arose to distinguish this species from it — the two are not botanically related. NC State separately flags confusion with the invasive Celastrus orbiculatus.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Poison block for Celastrus scandens, under the heading 'Poisonous to Humans:', rates Poison Severity as Low, with Poison Symptoms 'Vomiting, diarrhea, loss of consciousness, seizures,' Poison Toxic Principle 'Cardenolides, alkaloids,' Causes Contact Dermatitis 'No,' and a full Poison Part list of Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. NC State's Plant Type field carries the co-listed tag 'Poisonous,' its Edibility field reads 'Poison,' and its Problems field carries 'Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Weedy' — the Problem-for-Cats and Problem-for-Dogs values are cat/dog-scoped hazard flags separate from the human-scoped Poison block. RHS's dedicated page adds a handling warning NC State does not carry — 'Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.' — and names the pets at risk: 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten.' The sources disagree on scope: NC State lists the whole plant as poisonous, while Missouri Botanical Garden states only that 'Fruits are poisonous if ingested, but are considered to be quite tasty by many birds.' No source gives preparation instructions.
unknowns: RHS's dedicated page (rhs.org.uk/plants/101010/celastrus-scandens/details, title 'Celastrus scandens | American bittersweet') was reached by the audit after the researcher's guessed slug 404'd; its title and Potentially harmful field are cited at landing. Its Name Status value was not captured, so scientific_name_accepted stays null.

Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated page (plantfinder.mobot.org kempercode=a151) was reached by the audit after the researcher's search failed; its Common Name field, naming prose, Culture statement and fruit-only poison statement are cited at landing. Its Common Names tooltip list exists only in the link's markup and is not quoted.

Clemson HGIC, UGA fieldreport.caes.uga.edu, Penn State extension, UF/IFAS (edis/ask.ifas), and extension.umd.edu were checked for a Celastrus scandens page; none returned an accessible, confirmed species-specific page in this research pass, so no corroborating or conflicting light, soil, water, or dioecious-planting content from those domains could be cited. All non-NC-State-supported fields (scientific_name_accepted, chill_damage_f, day/night temperature fields, humidity fields, direct_sun_hours_max, soil_base beyond the generic outdoor garden_bed inference, soil_ph_min/max, water_regime and related watering fields, fertilize fields) are left null for lack of admissible-source support.

Dioecious-planting statements (need for separate male/female plants to fruit) were not found stated on the NC State page in the fetched content, and per task instructions such statements are not care values in any case, so none are included.

records.name_note: Naming splits across the admissible sources. NC State's page title carries a four-entry parenthetical (Great Rhododendron, Max, Rosebay Rhododendron, White Laurel) that its Common Name(s) list repeats in the same alphabetized order, so its structured list leads with "Great Rhododendron"; NC State's own body prose, however, leads with "Rosebay rhododendron," which this record follows. MoBot's dedicated page states a single Common Name value, "rosebay rhododendron," agreeing with NC State's prose, and its Noteworthy Characteristics adds "commonly called rosebay rhododendron or great laurel." RHS's dedicated page instead leads with "great laurel" and lists "American rosebay" under Other common names. This record follows MoBot's common-name field together with NC State's prose lead. "Great Rhododendron" and "White Laurel" appear only as alphabetized entries in NC State's list and are not used as the lead name in any source's running prose.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block (human-scoped, under its 'Poisonous to Humans:' heading, distinct from its Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags) rates Poison Severity as Low, with Poison Symptoms reading: "While the plants are known to contain toxins, ingestion of moderate amounts of azalea (nectar or leaves) poses little toxic hazard." (NC State's own text names "azalea" here even on this Rhododendron maximum page). The Toxic Principle is Grayanotoxins. Causes Contact Dermatitis is listed as No. The full Poison Part list is: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. NC State's Plant Type field also carries the Poisonous tag, and its Tags list separately carries #poisonous, #problem for cats, #problem for dogs, and #problem for horses — so pet risk is confirmed specifically for both cats and dogs (and also horses), independent of the human-scoped severity rating. Missouri Botanical Garden's cultivation notes add an unscoped whole-plant statement: "All parts of this plant are highly toxic if ingested," which does not itself name cats or dogs but corroborates the general hazard already established by NC State's cat/dog tags. RHS's Potentially harmful field for this species goes further than NC State's Low severity and its Causes Contact Dermatitis: No, stating: "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets (dogs, cats, rabbits, tortoises) Harmful if eaten..." — so the sources disagree on both severity and on whether handling requires protection, and RHS independently confirms the dog and cat scope.
unknowns: soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null: NC State's structured Soil pH field reads only 'Acid (<6.0)', an open-ended band with no closed range to derive a floor or ceiling from, and RHS's pH field lists only 'Acid' with no numeric range either, so there is no source-stated ceiling or floor to check in either direction.

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes full_sun even though NC State's structured Light field lists 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' as a tag: MoBot's structured Sun field for this species reads 'Part shade to full shade' (excluding full sun), and RHS's Position field lists only 'Partial shade,' so two of the three North American/UK structured fields exclude full sun and it is disclosed here rather than carried.

direct_sun_hours_max is left null: the only hour figures found are the generic hour ranges baked into NC State's site-wide Light-category legend ('6 or more hours...', '2-6 hours...'), not species-specific prose, so per the rules they cannot be used.

water_regime is set to keep_moist based on MoBot's cultivation-prose statement that 'Roots must never be allowed to dry out' together with NC State's body-prose preference for consistently moist, well-drained soil and its caution against overwatering (i.e., moist but not waterlogged). MoBot's own structured Water field reads only 'Medium,' a mid-scale value that per the rules cannot itself support keep_moist and is disclosed here as a counterpoint rather than used as the basis.

chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, day/night temperature fields, humidity fields, and light_fc fields are all left null: no admissible source for this species states a numeric damage-onset temperature, a day/night operating range, a humidity percentage or category, or a foot-candle light level — these sources describe hardiness zones, shade tolerance, and qualitative cultivation guidance only.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null: the only fertilizing guidance found is NC State's caution 'Avoid overwatering and over-fertilizing,' which gives no interval, active season, or dilution strength.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are left null per the rule that in-ground shrub watering is not framed with a dry-down target or day intervals in these sources.

is_houseplant is set to false on the strength of NC State's USDA Hardiness Zone range (3a-7b) and its native North American range description, indicating an outdoor landscape/woodland shrub; no source frames this species as an indoor houseplant.
